title: Scopes, Claims, Roles, and Policies
description: Learn how scopes limit token permissions, how claims describe users, and how .NET policies enforce authorization rules. Build a clean authorization model for APIs and SPAs.

data.text: Authentication tells you who a user is. Authorization decides what they can do. OAuth scopes, JWT claims, roles, and ASP.NET Core authorization policies are the tools that bridge this gap. Scopes limit what an access token can access. Claims carry attributes about the user. Roles group users by permission sets. Policies combine these into declarative rules that keep authorization logic out of your controllers.

Scopes are strings that represent permissions. When a client requests an access token, it specifies which scopes it needs. The authorization server includes only those scopes in the issued token. The resource server checks the scopes before processing the request. Common scope patterns include `read:orders` for read-only access, `write:orders` for mutations, and `admin` for full administrative access.

terms.definition: A permission string that limits what an access token can do, such as read:orders or write:profile.
A piece of information about a user, such as role, department, or email, carried in a token or identity.
A named group of permissions that simplifies assigning the same set of claims to multiple users.
A reusable, named set of requirements that determine whether a user can access a resource.

data.title: Scope-based API authorization
data.content: The API requires the orders:write scope for mutation endpoints.

data.text: Claims are the atomic facts about a user: their email, department, subscription tier, and roles. Roles are a special type of claim that groups users for authorization. In ASP.NET Core, the `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin,Manager")]` attribute checks for role claims. For more complex rules, authorization policies let you combine multiple requirements — for example, requiring both a role claim and a specific scope.

data.title: Authorization policies in .NET
data.content: Define policies at startup and apply them with attributes.

data.text: Sometimes a user's role is not enough — they should only be able to modify their own resources. Resource-based authorization evaluates the user's claims against a specific resource instance. ASP.NET Core provides `IAuthorizationService` and custom requirement handlers that can check ownership, document state, or any business rule.

data.title: Custom authorization requirement handler
data.content: Implement an IAuthorizationRequirement that checks if the user owns the resource.

data.text: In a React or Next.js frontend, authorization checks run in two places. First, the UI hides or shows elements based on the user's claims and roles — this is for usability, not security. Second, the backend API must enforce the same rules. Never rely on client-side authorization to protect data. The frontend should parse the ID token's claims and pass the access token in the Authorization header for every API call.

data.title: React role-based rendering
data.content: The UI conditionally renders buttons based on roles, but the API still enforces the rules.

items.text: Use scopes to limit API access to the minimum required permissions.
items.hint: A reporting service should request only read:reports, not admin.

items.text: Enforce authorization in policies, not scattered across controllers.
Use resource-based authorization for record-level access control.
items.hint: Roles alone cannot distinguish User A's record from User B's.

items.text: Repeat every authorization check on the backend, regardless of what the frontend shows.
items.hint: Client-side hiding is a usability feature, not a security boundary.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Scopes limit what an access token can do; claims describe the user; roles group permissions.
ASP.NET Core policies combine requirements into reusable authorization rules.
Resource-based authorization checks ownership on individual records.
Frontend authorization is for usability; backend authorization is for security.
data.takeaway: Authentication identifies, authorization decides. Apply the least privilege at every layer.
